name: Quiotepec Chinantec
confidence_why: Robbins 1961 is the only description that says where stress falls (on the first long syllable, otherwise on a short syllable with a tone glide, otherwise on the higher-toned of the first two syllables, otherwise on the second syllable), and the tonal studies of Castillo Martínez 2012 and Castellanos Cruz 2014 and 2021 contradict nothing but say nothing about word stress, so the rule rests on a single first-hand source whose author himself called it provisional.

catalog_quote: 3.12. There is a WORD STRESS (2), the placement of which, on the basis of the evidence so far observed, seems to be predictable when the borders and the phonemic content are known. Word stress seems normally louder than the crescendos and pulses described for word, syllable, and extension borders. Not every word of an utterance is equally stressed. The differences are presumably related to the phonological phrase, not discussed here (see 3.32 for the interplay of stress and tone). The first long syllable in a word is normally stressed: for example the second syllable in /. I'll ask. If there is no long syllable, a short syllable with a tone glide is stressed: the second syllable of /. beans. In the absence of either of these, stress falls on whichever of the first two syllables carries the higher tone: thus on the first syllable of /. bread, but on the second syllable of /. sea. In words with no long syllable, no tone glide, and identical tones on the first two syllables, the second syllable is stressed: /. singer.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: En cuanto al CHQ, la diferencia entre el llamado acento balístico y el acento controlado se corresponde con la duración de la vocal: el acento balístico con vocales breves mientras que el acento controlado con vocales largas. [...] Si la diferencia fuera acentual, se esperaría efectos sobre todos los elementos de la sílaba y no sólo sobre el núcleo vocálico. Como esto no ocurre así, de hecho, y la única diferencia vocálica notable es la duración, es mejor suponer que el contraste no es silábico, sino segmental [...] En conclusión, para el CHQ no se considera pertinente el análisis respecto a la distinción entre los llamados tonos balísticos y controlados, sino se concibe como una diferencia fonológica de duración vocálica.
new_statements.translation: As for CHQ [Quiotepec Chinantec], the difference between the so-called ballistic accent and the controlled accent corresponds to vowel duration: the ballistic accent with short vowels and the controlled accent with long vowels. [...] If the difference were accentual, effects would be expected on all the elements of the syllable and not only on the vocalic nucleus. Since this does not in fact happen, and the only notable vocalic difference is duration, it is better to assume that the contrast is not syllabic but segmental [...] In conclusion, for CHQ the analysis in terms of a distinction between so-called ballistic and controlled tones is not considered pertinent; rather it is conceived of as a phonological difference of vowel duration.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Quiotepec Chinantec is a tone language (6 level tones + contour/complex tones per Castillo; 4 primitive tones per Castellanos 2021) with predominantly monosyllabic words. The only 'accent' ever posited for it, Robbins' (1968) ballistic vs controlled accent, is explicitly rejected by all three modern descriptions as an accentual/prosodic distinction and reanalysed as a short vs long vowel contrast. No source states a positional word-stress rule; polysyllabic words (compounds, bu-prefixed nouns) are not treated for prominence.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Castillo 2012: 136 adds that the rejection of the ballistic/controlled analysis is for CHQ only and does not imply it is wrong for other Chinantec varieties. p. 191 notes Rensch (p.c.) suggested 3 tones ± accent instead of 6 levels, an analysis Castillo declines because 'qué condiciona la presencia o ausencia de acento' would be unexplained.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the syllable/word in isolation (monosyllabic citation forms, acoustic measurements). Words are mostly monosyllabic (Castillo 2012: 100; Castellanos 2014: 213; 2021: 101); bisyllables and trisyllables are compounds or bu- prefixed forms; tone in polysyllables is left for future work (Castillo 2012: 199). Sandhi and phrase-level tone are discussed but no phrase-stress claim is made.
new_statements.identity_note: All three theses describe the variety of San Juan Quiotepec (municipio San Juan Quiotepec, Sierra Juárez), Castillo and Castellanos being native speakers; this is the Glottolog quio1240 / ISO chq referent. Castellanos 2014 chs. 2-3 compare five Quiotepec-area communities (incl. Las Nieves, which the older literature treats separately, Freisigger et al. 1998). Glottolog's alternate names (Comaltepec Chinantec, Sierra Chinantec) should not be confused with coma1246 Comaltepec Chinantec, which Silverman's ballistic-syllable work describes.

new_statements.relation_note: Refines the catalog: the catalog and the existing Castillo 2012 statement class the language as tonal with a stress statement (Castillo reanalysing the ballistic/controlled 'accent' as a short/long vowel contrast, with no placement rule for polysyllables). Robbins 1961 supplies the only explicit placement rule on record: weight-first (long syllable), then tone-glide, then higher tone, then second syllable. It concerns word-level stress in polysyllabic words, not the ballistic/controlled contrast, so it does not contradict Castillo; both treat stress as non-contrastive. Confidence medium because the reading is from scanned (an earlier stage rendered the page scan of pp. 243-244 and reported…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and predictable from syllable weight and tone: the first long syllable of the word is stressed; if there is none, the short syllable bearing a tone glide; if neither, whichever of the first two syllables has the higher tone; if the first two syllables are equal on all counts, the second. Robbins hedges the rule as provisional ('on the basis of the evidence so far observed, seems to be predictable'). He adds (p. 244) that 'Not every word of an utterance is equally stressed. The differences are presumably related to the phonological phrase', and (pp. 246-248) that tone /4/ and falling contours in short syllables carry heavier stress and that stressed syllables tend to be higher in pitch.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none stated at word level; phrase-level differences in stress between words are mentioned but not described
new_statements.exceptions: Rule stated as normal ('normally stressed') and provisional; phrase-level stress differences deferred to an undescribed phonological phrase; stress and tone interact (§3.32).
new_statements.identity_note: All three listed works and Robbins 1961 concern Quiotepec Chinantec [chq] (SIL lists the Gardner & Merrifield chapter under subject language Quiotepec Chinantec [chq]); the existing Castillo 2012 statement is explicitly the variety of San Juan Quiotepec. Merrifield & Rensch 1990 is a multi-language volume (Comaltepec, Lealao, Quiotepec, Tepetotutla Chinantec); only its pp. 91-105 chapter is about this language.

new_statements.quote: A word consists of one or more syllables, only one of which is stressed. Morphemes belonging to major lexical classes (verbs, nouns, etc) are the source of stressed syllables. Most such morphemes are monosyllabic, but a few verbs and nouns have a pretonic syllable. Other pretonic syllables have their source in tense-aspect prefixes, directional prefixes based on motion verbs, and such like. [...] The POSTTONIC SYLLABLE [...] has its source in reduced (unstressed) forms of personal pronoun subjects (of verbs) and possessors (of nouns) or the affirmation modal [...] There are two kinds of word stress, BALLISTIC and CONTROLLED.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog codes Quiotepec as weight-hedged from Robbins 1961 §3.12 (word stress predictable: first long syllable, else the syllable with a tone glide). Gardner & Merrifield state the placement morphologically: the single word stress sits on the stem syllable of the noun/verb, prefixes are pretonic, pronoun enclitics posttonic. new_statements.rule_in_words: Each phonological word has exactly one stressed (tonic) syllable, and it is the syllable of the lexical morpheme (verb or noun stem, almost always monosyllabic); tense-aspect and directional prefixes (and the rare stem-internal first syllable) are pretonic and carry only single tones; reduced subject/possessor pronouns and the affirmation modal are posttonic enclitic syllables. The stressed syllable is either ballistic (surge and rapid decay of intensity, marked with an acute) or controlled (level intensity). The language is tonal (three single tones, four tone sequences on the tonic syllable).
new_statements.secondary_stress: none described: one stress per word; posttonic syllables carry only a relative higher/lower pitch, pretonic syllables only single tones
new_statements.exceptions: p. 100: after an open tonic syllable with a tone sequence, the third-person posttonic pronoun syllable has high pitch 'and the surge of intensity which is normally close to the beginning of the preceding tonic syllable is moved from its normal position to the posttonic syllable' (examples 'he pays it', 'he arrives', 'his house', 'his boss', 'his water'); p. 101 the possessed form of 'water' shows the same 'shift of stress and raising of tone of the posttonic syllable'; fn. 3 p. 93: Robbins treated the two kinds of checked syllable as long vs short rather than controlled vs ballistic
new_statements.identity_note: All three works describe the Chinantec of San Juan Quiotepec, Oaxaca (ISO chq); Gardner & Merrifield's principal speaker was Miguel García Martínez (age 17), son of Robbins' main teacher Ramón García Martínez; Robbins' data are from his own fieldwork in Quiotepec from the 1950s; the Merrifield & Rensch volume's other chapters concern Comaltepec, Lealao and Tepetotutla Chinantec.

new_statements.quote: 2.231. Accent. The phonetic actualization of accent is a combination of pitch and stress; it can be recognized by either or both (2.21). Accent is typically accompanied by relatively heavy stress; the peak of energy comes late in a long accented syllable [...] [p. 39:] The pitch of high tone in short syllables before the peak of a phonological word (Robbins, IJAL 1961, 3.12) is in the higher mid area, that of mid tone in the lower mid area [...] [p. 20:] Phonological units of a size-level larger than the syllable affect tone and accent, however: the way in which this works and the similar patterns of tonal morphophonemics that are morphemically defined are as yet unanalyzed.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's Robbins-1961 coding: the 1968 grammar keeps the 1961 notion of a predictable word peak by explicit reference (§3.12 of 1961) and adds, at the syllable level, a lexically contrastive 'accent' realised as pitch + heavy late stress on free syllables (the ballistic accent that Gardner & Merrifield 1990 call one of 'two kinds of word stress' and Castillo Martínez 2012 reanalyses as vowel length). It gives no new rule for which syllable of a polysyllabic word carries the word peak.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The 1968 grammar restates the 1961 syllable phonology and replaces the four-tone analysis by three tones plus a syllable 'accent' whose realisation is pitch plus relatively heavy, late-peaking stress; accent is a contrastive property of individual (free) syllables, kernels and extensions ('Accent does not occur in normal checked syllables', 'Accent does not occur in an interrupted syllable', 'Accent is limited to free syllables and to free kernels'), i.e. the entity later called the ballistic syllable. Word-level stress placement is not restated: the text refers to 'the peak of a phonological word (Robbins, IJAL 1961, 3.12)' and says that units larger than the syllable affect tone and accent in ways 'as yet unanalyzed'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: not discussed; §2.232 notes that unaccented mid-low 'pitch chameleon' syllables 'typically receive relatively heavy stress, though they are not accented' and that stress on some patterns is 'probably conditioned in part by intonation and its position in the phonological word or phrase' (p. 26)
new_statements.exceptions: accent has not been confirmed in any syllable whose only tone is low (p. 37); no accent contrast in checked or interrupted normal syllables (pp. 30-32)
new_statements.identity_note: All three works describe the Chinantec of San Juan Quiotepec, Oaxaca (ISO chq); Gardner & Merrifield's principal speaker was Miguel García Martínez (age 17), son of Robbins' main teacher Ramón García Martínez; Robbins' data are from his own fieldwork in Quiotepec from the 1950s; the Merrifield & Rensch volume's other chapters concern Comaltepec, Lealao and Tepetotutla Chinantec.

Aquí determinamos que el número 1 indica el tono bajo y el 6 el tono más alto.
tone_statements.translation: To mark the tones on the words of the list, written in Las Nieves Chinantec, I have used the tonal system we worked out with Dagmar and Thomas Smith (Freisinger et al. 1998), two linguists specialising in tone languages. There we determined that the number 1 indicates the low tone and 6 the highest tone.

readall_conflicts: No contradiction among opened sources. The only tension is one of object, not fact: Castillo Martínez 2012 (existing statement) denies an accentual ballistic/controlled contrast and reduces it to vowel length, while Robbins 1961 §3.12 posits a predictable, non-contrastive word stress in polysyllables whose first criterion is precisely syllable length (first long syllable), then tone glide, then the higher-toned of the first two syllables, else the second syllable. Both agree that stress is not contrastive; neither of the three listed works (Gardner & Merrifield 1990; Robbins 1968; Merrifield & Rensch 1990) could be opened, so whether the 1968 grammar or the 1990 tone chapter restates, revises, or drops the 1961 rule remains unverified. No disagreement on where the word peak falls, but the sources frame it differently: Robbins 1961 §3.12 (catalog, weight-hedged) predicts the stressed syllable from syllable content (first long syllable, else the syllable with a tone glide); Gardner & Merrifield 1990 §1 (works 0/1) state it morphologically (the single stressed syllable is the noun/verb stem; prefixes pretonic, reduced pronouns posttonic) and note one phonetic displacement (the intensity surge moves onto the posttonic third-person pronoun after an open syllable with a tone sequence, p. 100); Robbins 1968 (work 2) does not restate word-stress placement at all, referring back to 1961 §3.12, and instead introduces a contrastive syllable-level 'accent' (pitch + heavy late stress, fr…

sources.quote: A word consists of one or more syllables, only one of which is stressed. Morphemes belonging to major lexical classes (verbs, nouns, etc) are the source of stressed syllables. Most such morphemes are monosyllabic, but a few verbs and nouns have a pretonic syllable. Other pretonic syllables have their source in tense-aspect prefixes, directional prefixes based on motion verbs, and such like. [...] The POSTTONIC SYLLABLE [...] has its source in reduced (unstressed) forms of personal pronoun subjects (of verbs) and possessors (of nouns) or the affirmation modal [...] There are two kinds of word stress, BALLISTIC and CONTROLLED.
sources.locator: §1 'Word and syllable', p. 92 (p. 8 of; the scanned text); stress shift onto the posttonic pronoun §4, p. 100 (p. 16, the scanned text) and p. 101 (p. 17)
sources.note: SIL tone study of Quiotepec building on Robbins' tone + ballistic-accent analysis, with sandhi; likely explicit about accent in disyllables/phrases.

sources.quote: 2.231. Accent. The phonetic actualization of accent is a combination of pitch and stress; it can be recognized by either or both (2.21). Accent is typically accompanied by relatively heavy stress; the peak of energy comes late in a long accented syllable [...] [p. 39:] The pitch of high tone in short syllables before the peak of a phonological word (Robbins, IJAL 1961, 3.12) is in the higher mid area, that of mid tone in the lower mid area [...] [p. 20:] Phonological units of a size-level larger than the syllable affect tone and accent, however: the way in which this works and the similar patterns of tonal morphophonemics that are morphemically defined are as yet unanalyzed.
sources.locator: ch. 2 Phonology, printed pp. 21-40 (pp. 22-41): §2.21 'Reinterpretation of tone' pp. 24-26, §2.231 'Accent' p. 37 (p. 38, the scanned text), §2.233 p. 39 (p. 40, the scanned text) referring to the 1961 word-stress peak; §1.2 p. 20 (p. 21, the scanned text)
sources.note: The primary grammar; posits 3 tones + a ballistic 'accent' (pp. 15-25 per the theses) and, like Merrifield's Palantla grammar of the same series, may state where the accented syllable falls in polysyllabic phonological words; would supersede the second-hand summaries.

sources.citation: Robbins, Frank E. 1961. Quiotepec Chinantec syllable patterning. IJAL 27(3): 237-250.
sources.quote: 3.12. There is a worp stress (2), the placement of which, on the basis of the evidence so far observed, seems to be predictable when the borders and the phonemic content are known. [...] The first long syllable in a word is normally stressed: for example the second syllable in /y*+-nih*+-duh"/ I'll ask. If there is no long syllable, a short syllable with a tone glide is stressed: the second syllable of /ut+hnij?!/ beans. In the absence of either of these, stress falls on whichever of the first two syllables carries the higher tone [...]. In words with no long syllable, no tone glide, and identical tones on the first two syllables, the second syllable is stressed: /ti'+-?6/ singer.
sources.locator: §3.12, pp. 243-244 (archive.org scanned of IJAL 27(3), lines 8710-8747 of the; 'worp' in the scanned is the small-caps word)
sources.note: Named by the earlier scan; the first description of syllable types (ballistic/controlled) and prosodic patterning in the language.
